set1.io: Evaluate the patient’s response to oxygen therapy.
set1.q: A 59-year-old man with pneumonia is started on a simple mask. Thirty minutes later he is breathing more easily, his lips are pink instead of dusky, and his saturation is up to his target. Which is the next step in evaluating his response?
opts: Keep checking vitals and watch for complications

Correct. He looks better and his saturation reached his target, which covers symptom improvement, color and the objective saturation. Evaluating response also includes watching vital signs and monitoring further for complications, so ongoing checks are the next step, not a stopping point.
Stop oxygen now that he looks better

Stopping oxygen now would end the evaluation early. Response is judged by symptoms, work of breathing, color, saturation and vital signs, with further monitoring for complications. Tell: one good result starts the monitoring; it does not end it.
wrong stage or severity
Increase to a non-rebreather mask

A non-rebreather is a high-fraction device for severely hypoxic patients who are still ventilating well. He has improved to his target on a simple mask, so escalating would add oxygen he does not need. Tell: an improvement to target means keep the device and monitor.
reversed direction or value
Order a home oxygen qualification today

A home oxygen qualification documents hypoxia at rest, exertion or sleep and is performed at the time of need, when a patient is going home. It is not part of evaluating his response to oxygen for pneumonia. Tell: response evaluation is about how he is doing now; qualification is about home coverage.
wrong stage or severity

set1.io: Discuss the selection and application of oxygen delivery
set1.q: A 58-year-old man is placed on a non-rebreather mask at 10 L/min for severe hypoxia. The nurse notices the reservoir bag collapses completely each time he breathes in. Which adjustment is needed?
opts: Increase the flow until the bag stays inflated

Correct. The non-rebreather dosing rule is to prevent bag collapse on inspiration, within a flow of 10-15 L/min. His bag collapses completely on every breath at 10 L/min, the bottom of that range; with room up to 15 L/min, raising the flow within the range is the adjustment that works toward that rule.
Switch to a nasal cannula at 6 L/min

A nasal cannula at 6 L/min delivers at most 44%, far below the high fraction a severely hypoxic man needs. Switching would downgrade his oxygen when the real problem is flow into the bag. Tell: keep the mask and adjust its flow within 10-15 L/min.
wrong stage or severity
Remove the one-way valve

The one-way valve is what stops him from inhaling his own exhaled air, so removing it would defeat the purpose of the non-rebreather. The collapsing bag points to too little flow, not to the valve. Tell: the valve controls what he breathes in; the flow keeps the bag filled.
reversed direction or value
Lower the flow to 5 L/min

Lowering the flow to 5 L/min would take the mask below its 10-15 L/min range and work against the rule to prevent bag collapse. A severely hypoxic patient needs the high fraction the full flow gives. Tell: a collapsing bag is a reason to raise the flow, not lower it.
reversed direction or value

set1.io: Discuss the selection and application of oxygen delivery
set1.q: A 74-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has poor finger perfusion, and the pulse oximeter will not give a steady reading. His arterial oxygen pressure is 55 mm Hg on room air at rest. What is his home oxygen status?
opts: Qualifies in Group I

Correct. Documentation can use an arterial blood gas or pulse oximetry. An arterial oxygen pressure of 55 mm Hg or less qualifies at Group I, and his is 55, so he qualifies without the oximeter. Group I is recertified at 12 months.
Qualifies in Group II
Group II is for an arterial oxygen pressure of 56-59 mm Hg plus a comorbidity. His is 55, so he meets the Group I threshold directly. Tell: 55 or less is Group I; 56-59 is Group II.
adjacent fact
Cannot qualify without oximetry

The pulse oximeter is only one way to document hypoxia. The arterial blood gas is the other, and an arterial oxygen pressure of 55 mm Hg or less is the qualifying value. Tell: when oximetry fails, the blood gas can qualify him.
ruled out by a stated finding
Does not qualify at 55 mm Hg

His arterial oxygen pressure of 55 mm Hg is exactly at the qualifying value, since the criterion is 55 mm Hg or less, which includes 55. Tell: the cutoff includes the number 55, so he qualifies in Group I.
reversed direction or value

set1.io: Discuss the selection and application of oxygen delivery
set1.q: A 71-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is admitted with a flare. His oxygen saturation is 86% on room air, and the team wants to give him an exact, adjustable fraction of inspired oxygen rather than a fraction that changes with his breathing. Which delivery device is the best choice?
opts: Nasal cannula

A nasal cannula gives a fraction that varies with respiratory rate, inspiratory flow and tidal volume, and it is used mostly for mild hypoxia. Each added liter raises the fraction only about 4%, so it cannot be dialed in. Tell: a cannula is set by liters per minute, a Venturi mask by choosing a port.
ruled out by a stated finding
Simple mask

A simple mask is also a low flow device, and its fraction varies with respiratory rate, inspiratory flow and tidal volume. It is used for mild to moderate respiratory distress and gives no fixed fraction. Tell: the simple mask has no ports that lock in a fraction, so it cannot be dialed to an exact number.
ruled out by a stated finding
Venturi mask

Correct. He has chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and the team wants a precise, adjustable fraction of inspired oxygen that does not change with his breathing. The Venturi mask is an air-entrainment device: different ports set the fraction (24-50%), and it stays fixed whatever his demand.
Non-rebreather mask

A non-rebreather mask is a low flow device whose delivery varies with patient demand, so the fraction would drift as his breathing changes. It is meant for severe hypoxia with good ventilation, and his 86% is not that. Tell: a reservoir bag with a one-way valve means a variable fraction; ports mean a fixed one.
wrong stage or severity

set1.io: Discuss patient education for oxygen delivery
set1.q: A 77-year-old woman is going home on oxygen tanks. Her son asks what to do with the tanks and how to store them. Which property of the tanks drives the storage and disposal teaching?
opts: They hold compressed gas

Correct. Oxygen tanks contain compressed gas, and that property drives the teaching on proper storage and disposal. Her son should store the tanks as the teaching directs and not discard them as ordinary trash.
They hold a liquid fuel

The tanks hold compressed oxygen gas, not a liquid fuel. The flammability teaching is about oxygen supporting a fire, and storage and disposal rules follow from the compressed gas. Tell: the tank holds gas under pressure.
confused mechanism or drug class
They emit carbon monoxide
The tanks do not emit carbon monoxide. Carbon monoxide appears in the teaching only as a reason to have working carbon monoxide alarms. Tell: alarms detect it; tanks hold oxygen.
confused mechanism or drug class
They spoil within a week
Tanks do not spoil. The teaching is about proper storage and disposal because they contain compressed gas. Tell: the concern is pressure and flammability, not a shelf life.
common lay belief

set1.io: Discuss the selection and application of oxygen delivery
set1.q: A 70-year-old man admitted with a heart failure exacerbation still needs 2 L/min of oxygen on hospital day 1. His team plans to discharge him in a few days. When should his home oxygen qualification be performed?
opts: Once he no longer needs oxygen

Once he no longer needs oxygen there is no hypoxia left to document, and qualification rests on documented hypoxia at rest, with exertion or during sleep, performed at the time of need. He still needs 2 L/min now. Tell: qualify while the need is present, not after it resolves.
wrong stage or severity
After a year on home oxygen

Waiting a year is the interval for recertification in Group I, not for the first qualification. He needs his oxygen now and is going home soon, so qualification cannot wait. Tell: the 12-month mark is for renewing, not for starting.
reversed direction or value
At his first outpatient visit

His first outpatient visit comes after discharge, which would leave him without qualified oxygen at home. Documentation is performed at the time of need. Tell: the need arises as he leaves the hospital, so the qualification comes first.
wrong stage or severity
At the time of need, before discharge

Correct. The qualification is documented at the time of need, and he still needs 2 L/min with discharge planned in a few days. So the qualification is performed while he is in the hospital, before he leaves, so that home oxygen can be arranged.

set1.io: Discuss the selection and application of oxygen delivery
set1.q: A 58-year-old man with bronchitis is on a nasal cannula at 6 L/min with a saturation of 89%. He now has mild to moderate respiratory distress but is ventilating well. Which step fits his severity?
opts: Turn the cannula to 10 L/min
Turning a cannula to 10 L/min does not raise the fraction past its maximum of 44%, which is reached at 6 L/min. He is already there. Tell: if the cannula is at its ceiling, change the device.
reversed direction or value
Go straight to a bag-valve mask

A bag-valve mask is a resuscitator for a patient who is not ventilating. He is ventilating well, with only mild to moderate distress. Tell: the resuscitator is for failed ventilation, not for this severity.
wrong stage or severity
Stop oxygen and recheck in an hour

Stopping oxygen at 89% with distress would leave him hypoxic. He needs more oxygen, not less, and should move to the next device. Tell: persistent hypoxia with distress calls for escalation, not for a pause.
wrong stage or severity
Change to a simple mask at 5 to 10 L/min

Correct. He has mild to moderate respiratory distress, and his saturation of 89% persists on a cannula at 6 L/min, near the cannula's limit of 44%. A simple mask, a low flow device set at 5-10 L/min, is the step for this severity.

set1.io: Evaluate the patient’s response to oxygen therapy.
set1.q: A 65-year-old woman with chronic lung disease and a 60-year-old man with pneumonia are both on oxygen. The nurse asks what saturation target to use for each. Which principle applies?
opts: Both should be kept at 88%

Fixing both at 88% treats one target as universal. The target varies with the patient, so it cannot be applied to a woman with chronic lung disease and a man with pneumonia alike. Tell: a fixed shared number is the trap; the target is individualized.
adjacent fact
Both should match room air

Matching room air would make oxygen pointless in patients who have low saturations. The listed measure is an improved saturation toward a target set for each patient, not a return to room-air values. Tell: the target is set for the patient, not copied from room air.
common lay belief
The target varies with the patient

Correct. Response to oxygen is judged by saturation that improves to a target that varies with the patient. Her chronic lung disease and his pneumonia are different situations, so one number does not fit both, and each target is set for the patient.
Both should be kept at 100%

Keeping both at 100% ignores that the target varies. The listed measure is saturation that improves toward a target, and for a woman with chronic lung disease that target differs from a man with pneumonia. Tell: no single number applies to every patient.
common lay belief

set1.io: Identify the indications, benefits, and hazards of oxygen therapy.
set1.q: An 80-year-old man on home oxygen at 5 L/min by nasal cannula with no humidifier complains of a sore, dry nose and occasional bleeding. Which change addresses the cause?
opts: Apply a petroleum lip and nose balm

A petroleum-based balm is on the list of products to avoid with home oxygen, because oxygen is highly flammable. It would not be an appropriate treatment for his nose. Tell: petroleum products stay away from oxygen.
ruled out by a stated finding
Switch to a non-rebreather mask

A non-rebreather mask is a high-fraction device for severely hypoxic patients who are still ventilating well. He has a sore nose, not worsening hypoxia, and the mask would not solve it. Tell: his problem is dryness at a flow above 4 L/min.
wrong stage or severity
Add humidity to the oxygen

Correct. He is on 5 L/min by nasal cannula with no humidifier, and has a sore, dry nose with bleeding. That is mucosal irritation. Humidity is used with cannula flow rates greater than 4 L/min, so adding humidity to the oxygen treats the cause.
Increase the flow to 6 L/min
Raising the flow to 6 L/min keeps him above 4 L/min, where humidity is already needed and he has none. A higher flow leaves the missing humidity in place. Tell: fix the humidity, not the flow.
reversed direction or value

set1.io: Discuss patient education for oxygen delivery
set1.q: A 71-year-old man starting home oxygen asks why he must be so careful at home if oxygen is "just air." Which property of oxygen underlies the safety teaching?
opts: It is heavier than water
Oxygen being heavier than water is not a property stated and has no bearing on the teaching. The reason for the care is that oxygen is highly flammable. Tell: the key property is flammability.
common lay belief
It turns into carbon monoxide

Oxygen does not turn into carbon monoxide. Carbon monoxide appears in the teaching only as a reason for working carbon monoxide alarms. Tell: alarms detect carbon monoxide; flammability is the property of oxygen.
confused mechanism or drug class
It is highly flammable

Correct. Oxygen is highly flammable, which is why home oxygen teaching includes no smoking in the home, staying away from heat sources, avoiding petroleum products and posting signs. Oxygen is not just air, and fire is a listed hazard.
It is toxic to breathe for visitors
Oxygen is not described as toxic to visitors. The hazards listed are carbon dioxide retention, fire, mucosal irritation and vasoconstriction. Tell: the home safety teaching rests on flammability.
common lay belief

set1.topic: Reading the fraction from the flow
set1.io: Compare and contrast the different oxygen delivery systems.
set1.q: A 63-year-old woman with pneumonia is on a nasal cannula at 2 L/min. Her flow is increased to 5 L/min. About what fraction of inspired oxygen is she receiving now?
opts: 28% is her fraction at the old setting of 2 L/min. Her flow was increased by 3 liters, and each liter adds about 4%, so the new value is 12 points higher. Tell: 28% is the starting point, not the result.
adjacent fact

Correct. A nasal cannula at 2 L/min gives about 28%, and each added liter raises the fraction by about 4%. Going from 2 to 5 L/min adds 3 liters, which is 3 x 4% = 12%, so 28% + 12% = 40%. This matches the listed value of 40% at 5 L/min.
44% is the cannula's maximum, reached at 6 L/min. She is at 5 L/min, one liter below, so she is about 4% under that cap. Tell: 44% is the ceiling, not her setting.
adjacent fact

60% is above the nasal cannula's range, which tops out at 44%. Fractions of 60% and above come from reservoir-bag masks such as the non-rebreather at 10-15 L/min. Tell: a cannula cannot reach 60%, whatever the knob says.
reversed direction or value

set1.io: Explain the rationale for a nebulizer treatment.
set1.q: A 45-year-old man with a severe exacerbation of his chronic lung disease is too short of breath to use his inhaler properly. Which delivery method is preferred for his inhaled medication?
opts: An oropharyngeal airway

An oropharyngeal airway is an artificial airway that keeps the airway open in an unresponsive patient. He is breathing and using his inhaler, so he needs no airway device, only a different way to take his medicine. Tell: airways hold the passage open; a nebulizer delivers drugs.
adjacent fact
Nebulizer

Correct. He is in a severe exacerbation of chronic lung disease and too short of breath to use his inhaler properly. Inhalers are challenging in this situation, and a nebulizer delivers liquid medication directly to the airways without needing his coordination.
His usual inhaler, used faster

Using the inhaler faster does not fix the problem, since his breathlessness makes the technique itself unreliable. Inhalers are challenging in a severe exacerbation, which is a listed reason to switch to a nebulizer. Tell: the problem is the method under stress, not the speed.
common lay belief
A trach collar

A trach collar is an air-entrainment nebulizer interface for a patient with a tracheostomy. He has no tracheostomy, and the question asks about the preferred method for his inhaled medication, not the interface. Tell: the collar is a tracheostomy interface; the preferred method here is the nebulizer.
ruled out by a stated finding

set1.io: Evaluate the patient’s response to oxygen therapy.
set1.q: A 70-year-old woman with heart failure is started on oxygen. An hour later her arterial oxygen pressure has risen, but her arterial carbon dioxide has also risen and her pH has fallen. How should this response be read?
opts: A good response: pH is moving

The pH should correct toward normal for a good response, and hers fell. A falling pH alongside a rising carbon dioxide is moving the wrong way, not a sign of improvement. Tell: a good response needs the pH correcting, not just changing.
reversed direction or value
Cannot be judged without a chest film

Her blood gas already answers the question: arterial oxygen pressure, carbon dioxide and pH are the objective data for judging response. No chest film is needed to read this pattern. Tell: the gas values, not the imaging, decide whether the oxygen response is good.
adjacent fact
Not a good response: carbon dioxide is rising

Correct. A good response needs the arterial oxygen pressure to rise without a rise in arterial carbon dioxide, along with correction of the pH. Hers rose, but so did her carbon dioxide while the pH fell, so the oxygen is not working as it should and she needs close reassessment.
A good response: oxygen pressure has risen

A rising arterial oxygen pressure alone is not enough. The response is judged as an increase in arterial oxygen pressure without an increase in arterial carbon dioxide, plus correction of the pH. Tell: look at all three values; one improved value does not make a good response.
ruled out by a stated finding

set1.io: Discuss patient education for oxygen delivery
set1.q: A 72-year-old man starting home oxygen says he smokes on his back porch and that his wife smokes in the kitchen. Which teaching applies?
opts: His wife may smoke if he is in another room

Her smoking in another room does not remove the hazard. The teaching is no smoking in the home, because oxygen is highly flammable and fire is a listed hazard. Tell: the rule covers the home, not just the room with the tank.
common lay belief
Smoking is fine if the tank is turned off

A tank turned off still holds compressed gas, and oxygen tanks contain compressed gas. The teaching covers the home, not whether the flow is running. Tell: the rule is about the home environment, so flow status does not matter.
common lay belief
He must stop; visitors are exempt

Visitors are not exempt, since the rule is no smoking in the home. The hazard is that oxygen is highly flammable, and a visitor's cigarette ignites it the same way. Tell: the rule has no exemption for anyone who lights a flame in the home.
common lay belief
No one should smoke in the home

Correct. Home oxygen teaching is that oxygen is highly flammable, and no one should smoke in the home. His wife smokes in the kitchen, inside the home, so the rule applies to her, and the fire danger is the same whoever lights the cigarette.

set1.io: Discuss patient education for oxygen delivery
set1.q: A 79-year-old woman using home oxygen keeps an electric space heater beside her recliner, where she sits with her tubing. Which teaching applies?
opts: Lower her flow while the heater runs
Lowering her flow does not address the hazard. The teaching is about distance, at least 10 feet from heat sources, and has nothing to do with the flow rate. Tell: distance protects, not the knob.
common lay belief
Keep the heater 3 feet away
Three feet is far too close to an electric heater. The minimum distance from heat sources is at least 10 feet. Tell: the number to remember is 10 feet, so any smaller distance fails the teaching.
reversed direction or value
Keep oxygen at least 10 feet from the heater

Correct. Home oxygen teaching is to keep oxygen at least 10 feet from heat sources, including electric appliances as well as pilot lights and candles. A space heater beside her recliner is a heat source, so she must keep her oxygen at least 10 feet away.
A heater is safe because it has no flame
Lacking a flame does not make a heater safe. Electric appliances are listed heat sources, and oxygen is highly flammable. Tell: the rule covers electric appliances, not just flames.
common lay belief

set1.io: Identify the indications, benefits, and hazards of oxygen therapy.
set1.q: A 78-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has mild hypoxia, saturation 87%, during a cold. A student suggests a non-rebreather mask at 15 L/min "to be safe." Why should that be avoided?
opts: It cannot raise his saturation

A non-rebreather can raise his saturation; at 10-15 L/min it delivers 60-100%. The problem is that its high fraction is meant for severe hypoxia, and his is mild at 87%. Tell: this mask is powerful, which is why it is kept for severe hypoxia.
reversed direction or value
It causes vasoconstriction in the lungs

Vasoconstriction is the listed concern when oxygen is given in a myocardial infarction, not a lung effect in a cold. He has no cardiac event, and his issue is a device too strong for mild hypoxia. Tell: vasoconstriction goes with a myocardial infarction; severity decides the device.
adjacent fact
It is a fire hazard in hospitals

Fire is a listed hazard of any oxygen therapy, whichever device is used, so it is not a reason to avoid this mask in particular. The reason here is that the non-rebreather is for severe hypoxia and his is mild. Tell: a hazard shared by every device cannot single out one of them.
adjacent fact
It is meant for severe hypoxia

Correct. His hypoxia is mild at 87%, and a non-rebreather mask is used in severely hypoxic patients who are still ventilating well, delivering 60-100% at 10-15 L/min. For mild hypoxia the nasal cannula is the most commonly used device, so the non-rebreather overshoots his need.

set1.io: Discuss patient education for oxygen delivery
set1.q: A 68-year-old woman going home on oxygen asks what signs to post. Which signage is taught?
opts: A sign with her recertification date

Her recertification date is not a posted sign. Recertification is about keeping home oxygen qualified at 12 or 3 months, whereas signs are about safety in the home. Tell: dates belong in her chart; warnings belong on the wall.
adjacent fact
No Smoking and Oxygen in Use signs

Correct. Home oxygen teaching is to post No Smoking signage, and potentially Oxygen in Use signs, within the home. Oxygen is highly flammable, and the signs warn everyone who enters, including visitors and firefighters.
A sign with her oxygen flow rate

A sign with her oxygen flow rate is not part of the signage taught. The taught signs warn about smoking and oxygen use because of the fire hazard. Tell: signs are for warning others, not for recording her prescription.
adjacent fact
A sign with her pharmacy's number
The pharmacy's number is not part of the signage taught. The signs are No Smoking and, potentially, Oxygen in Use. Tell: signage addresses the fire hazard, not contact information.
common lay belief

set1.io: Explain the rationale for a nebulizer treatment.
set1.q: A 4-year-old boy with wheezing cannot coordinate pressing a metered-dose inhaler with breathing in, even with coaching. Which delivery method is the rationale for his medication?
opts: A larger-dose inhaler

A larger-dose inhaler is still an inhaler, and the problem is his coordination of pressing and breathing in, not the dose. Inhalers are challenging in certain situations, so more drug in the same device does not fix it. Tell: the barrier is the delivery method, so change the method.
common lay belief
A non-rebreather mask

A non-rebreather mask is an oxygen delivery device with a reservoir bag for severe hypoxia. It does not deliver liquid medication to the airways for wheezing. Tell: oxygen masks supply oxygen; a nebulizer delivers medication.
confused mechanism or drug class
A Venturi mask

A Venturi mask delivers a precise, fixed oxygen fraction (24-50%), not a medication. His difficulty is giving an inhaled drug, not delivering a set oxygen fraction. Tell: the Venturi mask controls oxygen; the nebulizer carries liquid medication to the airways.
confused mechanism or drug class
A nebulizer

Correct. A 4-year-old with wheezing cannot coordinate pressing a metered-dose inhaler with breathing in, even with coaching. Inhalers are challenging in certain situations, and a nebulizer delivers liquid medication directly to the airways without that coordination.

set1.topic: Reading the fraction from the flow
set1.io: Compare and contrast the different oxygen delivery systems.
set1.q: A 57-year-old man with bronchitis is placed on a simple mask at 6 to 7 L/min. About what fraction of inspired oxygen is he receiving?
opts: 28% is a nasal cannula value at 2 L/min. A simple mask at 6 to 7 L/min delivers more, and the listed value for that flow is 40%. Tell: 28% is a low cannula setting; the mask is higher.
adjacent fact

Correct. A simple mask is a low flow device set at 5-10 L/min, and its fraction depends on the flow: 5-6 L/min gives 35%, 6-7 L/min gives 40%, and 7-8 L/min gives 50%. At 6 to 7 L/min he is receiving about 40%.
50% is the simple mask's value at 7-8 L/min, one step higher than his setting. His 6 to 7 L/min corresponds to 40%. Tell: match the flow row; each row steps up by 5 or 10 points.
adjacent fact
80% is far above a simple mask's range of 35-50%. Those values belong to higher-flow, reservoir-bag devices such as the non-rebreather mask at 10-15 L/min. Tell: a simple mask cannot approach 80%.
reversed direction or value

set1.io: Discuss the selection and application of oxygen delivery
set1.q: A 55-year-old woman develops severe hypoxia, saturation 79%, from pneumonia. She is alert, breathing at a steady rate with good chest rise, and her arterial carbon dioxide is normal. Which device delivers the high fraction she needs?
opts: Non-rebreather mask

Correct. Her saturation of 79% is severe hypoxia, yet she is alert, breathing steadily with good chest rise, so she is still ventilating well. The non-rebreather mask is the device for severely hypoxic patients who are still ventilating well, giving 60-100% at 10-15 L/min through its reservoir bag.
Nasal cannula

A nasal cannula is a low flow device for mild hypoxia, and its fraction tops out at 44% even if the knob is turned higher. At 79% she needs a high fraction, which a cannula cannot supply. Tell: mild hypoxia and a ceiling of 44% point to the cannula; severe hypoxia with a reservoir bag points to the non-rebreather.
wrong stage or severity
Simple mask

A simple mask is meant for mild to moderate respiratory distress and delivers about 35-50% at 5-10 L/min. Her saturation of 79% calls for a higher fraction than that. Tell: the simple mask has no reservoir bag, while the non-rebreather has a bag that holds oxygen for the high fraction she needs.
wrong stage or severity
Bag-valve mask

A bag-valve mask is a resuscitator used to assist breathing for a patient who is not ventilating. She is alert, breathing at a steady rate with good chest rise, so she is breathing on her own. Tell: a bag-valve mask is for the patient who is not breathing adequately; this patient is ventilating well.
ruled out by a stated finding

set1.io: Discuss the selection and application of oxygen delivery
set1.q: A 69-year-old woman with chronic lung disease is assessed for home oxygen before discharge. Her resting room-air saturation is exactly 88%, and she has no other findings. What is her qualification?
opts: Group I, recertified at 12 months

Correct. Group I qualifies at a resting room-air saturation of 88% or less, and hers is exactly 88%, which meets the cutoff. Group I patients are recertified at 12 months, and no comorbidity is needed.
Group II, recertified at 3 months

Group II is for a saturation of 89% (or arterial oxygen pressure of 56-59 mm Hg) plus pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale or a hematocrit above 56%, recertified at 3 months. Her 88% already meets Group I. Tell: 88% or less is Group I; 89% needs a comorbidity.
adjacent fact
Not qualified without a comorbidity
A comorbidity is needed only when the saturation is 89%. At 88% she meets the Group I rest criterion as is. Tell: the boundary 88% counts; the comorbidity requirement begins at 89%.
wrong stage or severity
Qualified for exertion oxygen

Exertion oxygen requires a saturation of 88% or less with activity that improves with oxygen. No exertion testing is described, and her resting value already qualifies her at rest. Tell: she qualifies at rest, which is a stronger finding.
adjacent fact

set1.io: Discuss the selection and application of oxygen delivery
set1.q: A 73-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is ready for discharge after his treatment is optimized. His resting saturation on room air is 87%, and he has no pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale (right-sided heart failure from lung disease) or high hematocrit. How often will his home oxygen be recertified?
opts: Every 1 month

An interval of every 1 month is not one of the stated intervals. The two are 12 months for Group I and 3 months for Group II. Tell: only 12 months and 3 months appear as recertification intervals, and his criteria give 12.
reversed direction or value
Every 3 months

Every 3 months applies to Group II, the conditional group with a saturation of 89% plus pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale or a hematocrit above 56%. He has none of those and a saturation of 87% qualifies him as Group I. Tell: earlier recertification goes with a chronic complication.
adjacent fact
Every 12 months

Correct. His resting room-air saturation is 87%, at or below 88%, which is the Group I qualification (conditional Group II needs a comorbidity such as pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale or a hematocrit above 56%). Group I patients are recertified every 12 months.
Every 24 months

An interval of every 24 months is not stated either; Group I is recertified at 12 months and Group II at 3 months. Tell: with an uncomplicated resting saturation of 87%, the answer is the longer listed interval, 12 months.
reversed direction or value

set1.io: Evaluate the patient’s response to oxygen therapy.
set1.q: A 52-year-old woman with asthma is started on oxygen. She says she feels better, but her lips remain dusky, her accessory muscles are still working hard, and her saturation has not moved. How should her response be judged?
opts: Not yet adequate on clinical and objective measures

Correct. She feels better, but her lips are still dusky, her accessory muscles still work hard, and her saturation has not moved. Response is judged by symptoms, work of breathing, color and perfusion plus objective data. Most of those have not improved, so it is not yet adequate.
Adequate, because she feels better
Feeling better is only one of the clinical measures. Work of breathing and color have not improved, and the saturation has not moved. Tell: symptom relief alone does not make a response adequate.
ruled out by a stated finding
Adequate, because oxygen is running
Oxygen running is not a response. The response is judged by what happens to the patient: symptoms, work of breathing, color and objective saturation. Tell: delivery is not the same as effect.
common lay belief
Cannot be judged without a chest film

A chest film is not part of the listed response measures. The clinical and objective data she already has show the response is inadequate. Tell: the measures are symptoms, work of breathing, color, saturation and blood gas values.
adjacent fact

set1.io: Identify the indications, benefits, and hazards of oxygen therapy.
set1.q: A 62-year-old man with chest pain has a myocardial infarction with ST elevation. He is alert, with an oxygen saturation of 96% on room air. Which is the right approach to oxygen?
opts: Give a nasal cannula at 2 L/min

A nasal cannula is most commonly used in mild hypoxia, and at 96% he is not hypoxic. In a myocardial infarction oxygen is withheld unless the saturation is below 91%, so even a low dose is not called for. Tell: the rule depends on the saturation threshold, not the dose.
ruled out by a stated finding
Give a Venturi mask at 28%

A Venturi mask at 28% gives a precise fraction, but he has no hypoxia to correct. Oxygen in a myocardial infarction is held back unless the saturation is below 91%, because of vasoconstriction. Tell: precision matters when oxygen is needed; here none is.
ruled out by a stated finding
Withhold oxygen at this saturation

Correct. He is alert with a saturation of 96% on room air, well above the 91% threshold, and oxygen is not given in a myocardial infarction unless the saturation is below 91%, because oxygen causes vasoconstriction. With no hypoxia, no oxygen is the right plan.
Give a non-rebreather at 15 L/min

A non-rebreather at 15 L/min is a low flow device with a high fraction, used in severely hypoxic patients. His saturation is 96%, so this adds oxygen he does not need and risks vasoconstriction in a myocardial infarction. Tell: a normal saturation in a myocardial infarction means no oxygen, not a bigger device.
ruled out by a stated finding

set1.io: Select the appropriate equipment and supplies necessary for initiating oxygen therapy.
set1.q: A 57-year-old man with a chronic lung disease flare needs both inhaled medication by nebulizer and supplemental oxygen. He has no tracheostomy. Which air-entrainment interface over his face suits him?
opts: Nasal cannula

A nasal cannula is a low flow device that delivers oxygen only, and it is not an air-entrainment nebulizer interface. Tell: the cannula supplies oxygen; the aerosol mask supplies oxygen and nebulized medication.
adjacent fact
Aerosol mask

Correct. He needs a nebulizer for his inhaled medication along with oxygen, and he has no tracheostomy. The aerosol mask is an air-entrainment nebulizer interface that fits over the face, so it delivers oxygen and nebulized medication together.
Trach collar

A trach collar is the air-entrainment nebulizer interface that fits a tracheostomy. He has no tracheostomy, so the collar would not suit his face. Tell: the collar goes on a stoma; the aerosol mask goes over the face.
ruled out by a stated finding
Non-rebreather mask

A non-rebreather mask delivers oxygen through a reservoir bag and one-way valve, but it is not an air-entrainment nebulizer interface. It does not deliver nebulized medication. Tell: the reservoir bag means no nebulizer; the aerosol mask is the nebulizer interface.
adjacent fact

set1.io: Evaluate the patient’s response to oxygen therapy.
set1.q: A 64-year-old man with pneumonia has an arterial blood gas before and after starting oxygen. After oxygen, his arterial oxygen pressure is higher, his carbon dioxide is unchanged, and his pH has returned toward normal. How is this response read?
opts: A good response

Correct. A good response is an increase in arterial oxygen pressure without an increase in arterial carbon dioxide, plus correction of the pH. His oxygen pressure rose, his carbon dioxide stayed unchanged, and his pH moved back toward normal, which meets all three.
Carbon dioxide retention

Carbon dioxide retention would show a rising arterial carbon dioxide. His carbon dioxide is unchanged, so there is no sign of retention. Tell: unchanged carbon dioxide is what a good response requires.
ruled out by a stated finding
No response

His arterial oxygen pressure rose and his pH corrected, which are the objective signs of response. There is a response. Tell: rising oxygen pressure with correcting pH is the pattern of a good response.
reversed direction or value
A response if saturation reaches 100%

A saturation of 100% is not required. The saturation is judged against a target that varies with the patient, and his gas already shows a good response. Tell: the target varies, so 100% is not the goal.
common lay belief

set1.io: Identify the indications, benefits, and hazards of oxygen therapy.
set1.q: A 68-year-old woman with diabetes and an acute myocardial infarction has an oxygen saturation of 87% on room air. Which is the right approach to oxygen?
opts: Withhold oxygen because of vasoconstriction

Vasoconstriction is the reason oxygen is withheld in a myocardial infarction, but that applies unless the saturation is below 91%. At 87% she is below it, so the exception applies. Tell: withhold when the saturation is 91% or higher, give when it is below 91%.
wrong stage or severity
Wait for an arterial blood gas first

An arterial blood gas is not required before treating. A pulse oximeter reading of 87% already shows she is below 91%, and delaying oxygen leaves hypoxia uncorrected. Tell: the threshold rests on the saturation she already has; no extra test is needed to start.
wrong stage or severity
Withhold oxygen because of her diabetes

Diabetes is not a listed reason to withhold oxygen. The hazards listed are carbon dioxide retention, fire, mucosal irritation and vasoconstriction, and the myocardial infarction rule turns on a saturation under 91%. Tell: the saturation decides, not her comorbidity.
common lay belief
Give oxygen, since saturation is below 91%

Correct. Her saturation of 87% is below the 91% cutoff. Oxygen is held back in a myocardial infarction because of vasoconstriction, but only while the saturation is 91% or higher. She is hypoxic, so the benefit of correcting hypoxia wins and she should receive oxygen.

set1.io: Discuss the selection and application of oxygen delivery
set1.q: A 48-year-old woman with influenza has mild to moderate respiratory distress and a saturation of 88%. She keeps mouth-breathing because her nose is congested. Which device suits her level of distress and delivers through both nose and mouth?
opts: Nasal cannula

A nasal cannula delivers only through the nostrils, so her congested nose and mouth breathing would waste much of the oxygen. It is the usual choice for mild hypoxia, not for this level of distress. Tell: the cannula sits in the nose; the simple mask covers the nose and mouth.
ruled out by a stated finding
Non-rebreather mask

A non-rebreather mask also covers both nose and mouth, but it is reserved for severely hypoxic patients who are still ventilating well, using a reservoir bag at 10-15 L/min. She is only mildly to moderately distressed at 88%. Tell: the reservoir bag means a high fraction for severe hypoxia; the simple mask has no bag.
wrong stage or severity
Trach collar

A trach collar is an air-entrainment nebulizer interface that fits over a tracheostomy, so it delivers to the airway through the stoma, not through the nose and mouth. She has no tracheostomy. Tell: the collar goes on a tracheostomy; the mask goes over the face.
ruled out by a stated finding
Simple mask

Correct. She has mild to moderate respiratory distress with a saturation of 88%, and with a congested nose she breathes through her mouth. A simple mask is a low flow device for mild to moderate distress that covers nose and mouth, so oxygen reaches her whichever way she breathes.

set1.io: Discuss the selection and application of oxygen delivery
set1.q: A 72-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has a daytime saturation of 93%. Overnight oximetry shows his saturation falling to 87% for long stretches. What does he qualify for?
opts: Oxygen during exertion

The exertion criterion needs a saturation of 88% or less with activity that improves with oxygen. His problem was documented overnight, not with walking. Tell: look at when the low value was recorded; here it was during sleep.
adjacent fact
Nocturnal oxygen

Correct. His daytime saturation of 93% is normal, but overnight it falls to 87%. The sleep criterion is a saturation of 88% or less with a drop of 5% or more from baseline: 87% is under 88%, and 93 minus 87 is a 6% drop. He qualifies for nocturnal oxygen.
Continuous oxygen at rest

Continuous oxygen at rest requires a resting room-air saturation of 88% or less. His daytime value is 93%, so he does not qualify for that. Tell: the abnormal reading occurs only overnight, so the qualification is for sleep.
ruled out by a stated finding
Nothing, since daytime is normal

A normal daytime reading does not close the question, because qualification is documented at rest, with exertion and with sleep. His overnight values meet the sleep criterion. Tell: a normal day value with a low overnight value points to sleep qualification.
wrong stage or severity

set1.io: Discuss the selection and application of oxygen delivery
set1.q: A 62-year-old woman with pneumonia is on a Venturi mask. She is breathing fast and deep, and her saturation dips each time she takes a big breath. Which dosing principle is being violated?
opts: The fraction must stay under 0.50

Staying under 0.50 is the recommendation for the air-entrainment nebulizer. The Venturi mask's own range is 24-50%, and her problem is the dips with each breath, not the fraction setting. Tell: the ceiling of 0.50 is about the nebulizer; her dips point to flow versus demand.
adjacent fact
Total flow must exceed inspiratory demand

Correct. The Venturi mask is an air-entrainment device that delivers a fixed fraction only if the total flow stays higher than her inspiratory demand. She is breathing fast and deep and her saturation dips with big breaths, which suggests her demand exceeds the flow.
The bag must not collapse on inspiration

Preventing bag collapse on inspiration is the dosing principle for the non-rebreather mask. A Venturi mask has no reservoir bag. Tell: bag collapse belongs to the non-rebreather; total flow versus demand belongs to the Venturi mask.
adjacent fact
Humidity is needed above 4 L/min

Humidity is used with nasal cannula flow rates greater than 4 L/min. It is a nasal cannula principle and does not explain her saturation dipping on deep breaths. Tell: humidity protects the nose; flow versus demand keeps the fraction fixed.
adjacent fact

set2.io: Discuss the selection and application of oxygen delivery
set2.q: A 67-year-old woman with lung disease is being assessed for home oxygen. Her resting room-air saturation is 92%. Which is the next step in her qualification?
opts: Order a complete blood count

A complete blood count would give a hematocrit, which matters only as a comorbidity for a resting saturation of 89% or an arterial oxygen pressure of 56-59 mm Hg. Her resting value of 92% is above both, so the hematocrit is not the next step. Tell: test exertion before looking for comorbidities.
adjacent fact
Check her saturation with exertion

Correct. A resting saturation of 92% is above the 88% rest cutoff, so rest alone does not qualify her. Qualification is documented during rest, exertion and/or sleep, so the next step is to check her saturation with exertion (and sleep if indicated).
Stop: she does not qualify

Stopping at the resting value ignores that hypoxia can be documented with exertion or during sleep. A resting 92% only means she does not meet the rest criterion. Tell: a normal rest value leaves exertion and sleep to be tested.
wrong stage or severity
Prescribe oxygen at 2 L/min now

Prescribing oxygen now has no documented hypoxia behind it. A saturation of 92% at rest does not meet the rest criterion of 88% or less, and a qualifying low value must first be documented. Tell: document first, then prescribe.
wrong stage or severity

set2.io: Identify the indications, benefits, and hazards of oxygen therapy.
set2.q: A 67-year-old man on home oxygen for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease arrives with burns to his lips and nose after lighting a cigarette while wearing his cannula. Which hazard does this show?
opts: Mucosal irritation

Mucosal irritation is dryness or soreness of the nasal lining from oxygen, usually at higher flows without humidity. It does not involve burns from an ignition source. Tell: dry, irritated mucosa is mucosal irritation; burns after a lit cigarette are fire.
adjacent fact
Vasoconstriction

Vasoconstriction is the effect of oxygen in a myocardial infarction, not a burn mechanism. His injury came from an open flame. Tell: a burn from an ignition source is fire; vasoconstriction is a cardiac concern when oxygen is not needed.
adjacent fact
Fire

Correct. A man on home oxygen lights a cigarette while wearing his cannula and burns his lips and nose. Oxygen is highly flammable, and fire is a listed hazard of oxygen therapy, which is why no smoking is taught for every home oxygen user.
Hypercapnia

Hypercapnia, or carbon dioxide retention, is a listed hazard of oxygen, but it is retained gas, not a burn. His injury is burns after a lit cigarette. Tell: burns from a flame mean fire, not carbon dioxide.
adjacent fact

set2.io: Identify the indications, benefits, and hazards of oxygen therapy.
set2.q: A 67-year-old man has a myocardial infarction and is placed on oxygen in the ambulance although his saturation was 98%. Which effect of oxygen makes this a problem?
opts: Vasoconstriction

Correct. His saturation was 98%, so he was not hypoxic. Oxygen is not given in a myocardial infarction unless the saturation is below 91%, because oxygen causes vasoconstriction. Giving it to a man with a normal saturation exposes him to that effect without benefit.
Carbon dioxide retention

Carbon dioxide retention is a listed hazard of oxygen, but it is not the reason oxygen is withheld in a myocardial infarction; that reason is vasoconstriction. Tell: the myocardial infarction rule points to vasoconstriction.
adjacent fact
Mucosal irritation

Mucosal irritation is the dryness and soreness of the nose from oxygen, especially without humidity at higher flows. It does not explain why oxygen is avoided in a myocardial infarction. Tell: irritation is local; vasoconstriction is the cardiac concern.
adjacent fact
Fire risk

Fire risk is real around any oxygen, but it does not explain why oxygen is withheld at a saturation of 98% in a myocardial infarction. Tell: the myocardial infarction caution is about vasoconstriction, not ignition.
adjacent fact

set2.io: Discuss patient education for oxygen delivery
set2.q: A 69-year-old woman on home oxygen has dry, cracked lips and uses a petroleum jelly lip balm several times a day. Which teaching applies?
opts: Use more balm to protect the lips

Using more balm adds more of what home oxygen teaching says to avoid: petroleum-based lip balms, lotions, oils and grease. Dry lips do not change that. Tell: protecting the lips with a petroleum product conflicts with oxygen safety.
reversed direction or value
Switch her oxygen to a non-rebreather

A non-rebreather mask is a high-fraction device for severely hypoxic patients who are still ventilating well. Dry lips are not an indication to switch, and the mask would not address the balm. Tell: her issue is a product, not the delivery device.
adjacent fact
Stop her home oxygen

Stopping her oxygen is not called for. The teaching is to avoid petroleum-based products while keeping oxygen use safe, not to discontinue oxygen. Tell: remove the hazard, which is the balm, and keep the oxygen.
wrong stage or severity
Stop using petroleum-based products

Correct. Petroleum-based products such as lip balms, lotions, oils and grease are to be avoided with home oxygen. Her petroleum jelly lip balm, used several times a day, is exactly that, so she should stop it. Her dry lips are not a reason to keep using it.

set2.io: Discuss patient education for oxygen delivery
set2.q: A 74-year-old man on home oxygen has a gas water heater with a pilot light in the hallway where he likes to sit. How far from it should his oxygen be kept?
opts: At least 2 feet
Two feet is far short of the stated distance. Oxygen is highly flammable, and the minimum from heat sources such as pilot lights is at least 10 feet. Tell: the distance in the teaching is 10, not 2.
reversed direction or value
At least 5 feet
Five feet is only half the stated minimum. The teaching specifies at least 10 feet from heat sources, and a pilot light is a flame. Tell: if the number is smaller than 10 feet, it is too close.
reversed direction or value
At least 10 feet

Correct. Home oxygen teaching is to keep oxygen at least 10 feet from heat sources, which include pilot lights, electric appliances and candles. A gas water heater with a pilot light sits in the hallway where he sits, so his oxygen must be kept at least 10 feet away.
At least 50 feet

Fifty feet is farther than the stated minimum, and it would be impractical inside a home. The teaching gives at least 10 feet from heat sources. Tell: the guideline is a minimum of 10 feet, not a vague large distance.
reversed direction or value

set2.io: Discuss the selection and application of oxygen delivery
set2.q: A 70-year-old woman with interstitial lung disease, pulmonary hypertension and a hematocrit of 52% has a resting room-air saturation of 89%. Which finding makes her qualify?
opts: Nothing; 89% does not qualify

At 89% alone she would not qualify, but she does not stand on 89% alone. Her pulmonary hypertension adds the comorbidity that makes the saturation qualify. Tell: 89% plus a listed comorbidity qualifies.
ruled out by a stated finding
Her pulmonary hypertension

Correct. Her resting saturation of 89% is just above the Group I cutoff of 88%, so she needs a comorbidity. Pulmonary hypertension is one of the listed qualifying findings, so it makes her qualify as Group II.
Her hematocrit of 52%
A hematocrit of 52% is below the threshold of above 56% needed for polycythemia to count. It does not qualify her. Tell: the hematocrit must be above 56%.
reversed direction or value
Her interstitial lung disease

Interstitial lung disease is not one of the qualifying comorbidities. The list is pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale and a hematocrit above 56%. Tell: it is the complications, not the lung diagnosis, that count.
adjacent fact

set2.io: Identify the indications, benefits, and hazards of oxygen therapy.
set2.q: A 71-year-old woman with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has a myocardial infarction. Her saturation is 93% on room air. A colleague wants to start oxygen by nasal cannula. Which is the right call?
opts: Hold oxygen at a saturation of 93%
Correct. Oxygen is not given in a myocardial infarction unless the saturation is below 91%, because of vasoconstriction. Her saturation of 93% is above that, so oxygen is held.
Start the nasal cannula at 2 L/min

A cannula at 2 L/min (about 28%) is a low dose, but the dose is not the issue. In a myocardial infarction oxygen is withheld unless the saturation is below 91%, and hers is 93%. Tell: the threshold decides first, then the device.
ruled out by a stated finding
Start a Venturi mask for her lung disease

A Venturi mask is often used in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease for its precision, but precision matters only when oxygen is needed. Her saturation of 93% is above the 91% line in a myocardial infarction. Tell: choosing a device comes after deciding that oxygen is needed.
adjacent fact
Start a non-rebreather mask

A non-rebreather delivers 60-100% and is used in severely hypoxic patients. She is at 93%, above the 91% line in a myocardial infarction, so no device is called for. Tell: no hypoxia means no oxygen, and certainly not a high-fraction mask.
wrong stage or severity

set2.io: Compare and contrast the different oxygen delivery systems.
set2.q: A 75-year-old woman with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is on a nasal cannula. Her breathing rate and depth change constantly, and her saturation swings with them. Which delivery system would hold her fraction of inspired oxygen steady?
opts: A non-rebreather mask

A non-rebreather mask delivers a high fraction from its reservoir bag, but its fraction still varies with patient demand. It would raise her oxygen without making it steady. Tell: of the listed devices, only the air-entrainment system has a fixed fraction.
confused mechanism or drug class
A partial rebreather mask

A partial rebreather mask also uses a reservoir bag, and some exhaled gas gets into it; its fraction varies with patient demand. It is also not commonly used in a clinical setting. Tell: a reservoir bag raises the fraction; air entrainment is what fixes it.
common lay belief
A simple oxygen mask

A simple oxygen mask covers nose and mouth, but like the cannula its fraction varies with respiratory rate, inspiratory flow and tidal volume. Switching to it would leave the swings in place. Tell: mask shape does not fix the fraction; air entrainment does.
adjacent fact
An air-entrainment system

Correct. A nasal cannula's fraction varies with respiratory rate, inspiratory flow and tidal volume, which is why her saturation swings as her breathing changes. An air-entrainment system gives a fixed fraction that does not fluctuate with patient demand, so it would hold her fraction steady.

set2.io: Discuss the selection and application of oxygen delivery
set2.q: A 69-year-old man with pneumonia is on a nasal cannula. His nurse turned the flow up to 8 L/min and his saturation is still 84%. He is alert and still ventilating well. Which is the next step?
opts: Turn the cannula up to 12 L/min

A cannula can be turned past 6 L/min, but the fraction stays capped at 44%. Going from 8 to 12 L/min would add no oxygen to his 84% and would dry his nose further. Tell: if more liters of cannula flow no longer raise the fraction, change the device, not the knob.
reversed direction or value
Add a second nasal cannula

A second nasal cannula is not a device that raises the fraction: a cannula's fraction is capped at 44% whatever the flow. He needs a higher fraction than that, which comes from a different device. Tell: his problem is the ceiling of the cannula itself, so the fix is a reservoir-bag mask.
common lay belief
Lower the flow to 2 L/min

Lowering the flow to 2 L/min would drop the fraction to about 28% and make his hypoxia worse. His saturation is already low at 84%, so he needs more oxygen, not less. Tell: lower flows are for mild hypoxia on a cannula; he has outgrown it.
reversed direction or value
Change to a non-rebreather mask

Correct. His cannula is already above its limit: the cannula covers 1-6 L/min and its fraction tops out at 44%, so more turning gains nothing. He is still at 84% and still ventilating well, which is the listed use of the non-rebreather mask: severely hypoxic patients who are still ventilating well. At 10-15 L/min it delivers 60-100%, well above the cannula's ceiling.

set2.io: Discuss the selection and application of oxygen delivery
set2.q: A 66-year-old man with heart disease and type 2 diabetes has a resting room-air saturation of 89%. He has no pulmonary hypertension, no cor pulmonale (right-sided heart failure from lung disease), and his hematocrit is 44%. Does he qualify for home oxygen at rest?
opts: Yes, because his hematocrit is high
His hematocrit is 44%, well below the 56% needed for polycythemia to count. The comorbidity criterion needs a hematocrit above 56%. Tell: a high hematocrit would help, but 44% is not high.
reversed direction or value
No, 89% needs a listed comorbidity

Correct. A resting saturation of 89% is above the 88% cutoff, so it needs a listed comorbidity: pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale or a hematocrit above 56%. He has none, and his hematocrit is only 44%. Heart disease and diabetes are not on the list, so he does not qualify at rest.
Yes, in Group I
Group I needs a saturation of 88% or less (or arterial oxygen pressure of 55 mm Hg or less) at rest. At 89% he is above the cutoff. Tell: Group I starts at 88%; his 89% does not meet it.
wrong stage or severity
Yes, in Group II because of diabetes

Diabetes is not one of the qualifying comorbidities. Group II requires pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale or a hematocrit above 56% together with a saturation of 89%. Tell: look for a lung-related complication or polycythemia, not general comorbidities.
adjacent fact

set2.io: Discuss the selection and application of oxygen delivery
set2.q: A 68-year-old woman who smoked for 40 years has an arterial oxygen pressure of 57 mm Hg at rest on room air and a hematocrit of 58%. Which recertification interval applies to her home oxygen?
opts: Every 1 month

An interval of every 1 month is not one of the stated intervals. Group I is recertified at 12 months and Group II at 3 months, and her profile is Group II. Tell: only 12 and 3 appear, and a complication shifts the answer to 3.
reversed direction or value
Every 3 months

Correct. Her arterial oxygen pressure of 57 mm Hg lies in the 56-59 range, above the Group I limit of 55 mm Hg, so she needs a comorbidity. Her hematocrit of 58% is above 56%, which is polycythemia. That puts her in Group II, which is recertified every 3 months.
Every 12 months

Every 12 months is the Group I interval, which needs a pressure of 55 mm Hg or less. Hers is 57 mm Hg, above that, and she qualifies only because of her high hematocrit. Tell: the comorbidity-dependent group recertifies sooner.
adjacent fact
Every 24 months

An interval of every 24 months is not stated; the longest is 12 months, for Group I. She is Group II with polycythemia, so her interval is shorter, not longer. Tell: complications shorten the interval.
reversed direction or value

set2.io: Identify the indications, benefits, and hazards of oxygen therapy.
set2.q: A 70-year-old woman on a nasal cannula at 6 L/min without humidification develops nosebleeds and a sore, crusted nose. Which hazard of oxygen therapy is this?
opts: Hypercapnia

Hypercapnia, or carbon dioxide retention, is a listed hazard, but it is not a local nasal problem. Her problem is local to the nose, with bleeding and crusting. Tell: hypercapnia is retained carbon dioxide; mucosal irritation is local to the nose.
adjacent fact
Vasoconstriction

Vasoconstriction is the listed concern with oxygen in a myocardial infarction. She has no cardiac event, and her findings are local nasal bleeding and crusting. Tell: vasoconstriction belongs with a myocardial infarction; dry, bleeding nasal mucosa belongs with mucosal irritation.
adjacent fact
Oxygen toxicity of the lungs

Oxygen toxicity of the lungs is not among the listed hazards, which are carbon dioxide retention, fire, mucosal irritation and vasoconstriction. Her signs are in the nose, not the lungs. Tell: the listed hazard that affects the nose and airway lining is mucosal irritation.
adjacent fact
Mucosal irritation

Correct. She has been on 6 L/min through a nasal cannula without humidification, and now has nosebleeds and a sore, crusted nose. Dry oxygen irritating the nasal lining is mucosal irritation, a listed hazard. Humidity is used when the flow is greater than 4 L/min.

set2.io: Select the appropriate equipment and supplies necessary for initiating oxygen therapy.
set2.q: A 72-year-old man with a long-term tracheostomy after head and neck cancer needs humidified supplemental oxygen at home. Which interface delivers air-entrainment nebulizer oxygen to his airway?
opts: Simple mask

A simple mask is a low flow device that covers the nose and mouth. It is not an air-entrainment nebulizer interface, and it would sit over a stoma he breathes through. Tell: the simple mask is a face interface with a variable fraction; the trach collar is the airway interface on this system.
ruled out by a stated finding
Open face mask

An open face mask is an air-entrainment nebulizer interface, but it sits over the face, as does the aerosol mask. A man who breathes through a tracheostomy needs the interface that fits the stoma. Tell: face interfaces are the aerosol and open face masks; the stoma interface is the trach collar.
adjacent fact
Trach collar

Correct. He has a long-term tracheostomy and needs humidified oxygen delivered by an air-entrainment nebulizer. The trach collar is the air-entrainment nebulizer interface that fits over a tracheostomy, so it delivers to his airway directly.
Nasal cannula

A nasal cannula sits in the nostrils, which would not reach a patient breathing through a tracheostomy, and it is a low flow device, not an air-entrainment one. Tell: the cannula is a nose device; the trach collar is the tracheostomy device.
ruled out by a stated finding

set2.io: Discuss the selection and application of oxygen delivery
set2.q: A 70-year-old woman with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and an echocardiogram showing pulmonary hypertension has a resting room-air saturation of 89%. Which statement about home oxygen applies to her?
opts: She qualifies in Group II

Correct. Her resting saturation of 89% is above the Group I cutoff of 88% or less, so on its own it would not qualify. The echocardiogram showing pulmonary hypertension adds the comorbidity that makes a saturation of 89% qualify, which is Group II (recertified at 3 months).
She qualifies in Group I

Group I requires a saturation of 88% or less (or arterial oxygen pressure of 55 mm Hg or less) at rest. At 89% she is just above that, so she falls into the conditional group. Tell: 88% or less is Group I; 89% needs a comorbidity and is Group II.
wrong stage or severity
She does not qualify at 89%

She does qualify: a saturation of 89% plus pulmonary hypertension meets Group II criteria. The 89% alone would not, but the comorbidity changes the answer. Tell: 89% by itself fails, but 89% plus pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale or a hematocrit above 56% qualifies.
ruled out by a stated finding
She qualifies for sleep oxygen alone

Her qualifying finding is at rest, not during sleep. The sleep criterion is a saturation of 88% or less with a drop of 5% or more from baseline, and nothing here describes sleep. Tell: sleep oxygen requires a documented overnight drop; her stem gives a resting value.
adjacent fact

set2.io: Identify the indications, benefits, and hazards of oxygen therapy.
set2.q: A 34-year-old man is brought in after running a generator in a closed garage. He has a headache and is confused; pulse oximetry reads 98%. Which treatment is indicated?
opts: Oxygen therapy

Correct. After exposure to generator exhaust in a closed garage, his headache and confusion fit carbon monoxide poisoning, which is a listed indication for oxygen therapy. The normal reading of 98% does not remove that indication, so oxygen is the treatment.
No oxygen, since saturation is normal

A normal saturation does not rule out oxygen here, because carbon monoxide poisoning is itself a listed indication, along with hypoxia, perioperative needs, air hunger and cluster headache. Tell: when the indication is poisoning, the reading of 98% is not the deciding clue.
ruled out by a stated finding
A nebulized bronchodilator

A nebulized bronchodilator delivers liquid medication to the airways, and nothing in his story suggests airway disease. His headache and confusion follow exposure to exhaust in a closed space. Tell: nebulizers treat airway problems; carbon monoxide poisoning is treated with oxygen.
confused mechanism or drug class
Breathing into a paper bag

Breathing into a paper bag is not a therapy for this exposure. Carbon monoxide poisoning is listed among the respiratory conditions for which oxygen therapy is indicated. Tell: the exhaust exposure in a closed garage calls for oxygen, not rebreathing.
common lay belief

set2.io: Discuss the selection and application of oxygen delivery
set2.q: A 71-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and cor pulmonale (right-sided heart failure from lung disease) has an arterial oxygen pressure of 58 mm Hg at rest. What is his qualification status?
opts: Group I, recertified at 12 months

Group I requires an arterial oxygen pressure of 55 mm Hg or less (or a saturation of 88% or less) at rest and is recertified at 12 months. His 58 mm Hg is above that, so he qualifies only through his comorbidity. Tell: 55 or less is Group I; 56-59 plus a comorbidity is Group II.
adjacent fact
Not qualified at 58 mm Hg

He does qualify: 58 mm Hg falls in the 56-59 range, and cor pulmonale is a qualifying comorbidity. The pressure alone would fall short, but together they meet Group II. Tell: the middle range qualifies once a listed comorbidity is present.
ruled out by a stated finding
Qualified for sleep oxygen

His data are resting values, and sleep qualification needs a saturation of 88% or less with a drop of 5% or more from baseline. Nothing about sleep is described. Tell: this is a resting qualification with a comorbidity.
adjacent fact
Group II, recertified at 3 months

Correct. His arterial oxygen pressure of 58 mm Hg is above the Group I limit of 55 mm Hg but within the 56-59 range, which qualifies only with a comorbidity. He has cor pulmonale, so he is Group II, and Group II is recertified at 3 months.

set2.io: Select the appropriate equipment and supplies necessary for initiating oxygen therapy.
set2.q: A 46-year-old woman with mild hypoxia, saturation 89%, had both nostrils packed for a severe nosebleed. She is comfortable otherwise. Which device suits her mild hypoxia with her nose blocked?
opts: Trach collar
A trach collar is an air-entrainment nebulizer interface for a patient with a tracheostomy. She has no tracheostomy. Tell: the collar fits a stoma; the mask fits the face.
ruled out by a stated finding
Non-rebreather at 15 L/min

A non-rebreather at 15 L/min also covers the face, but it is for severely hypoxic patients who are still ventilating well. Her hypoxia is mild at 89%, so it overshoots. Tell: match the device to severity: mild to moderate points to the simple mask.
wrong stage or severity
Simple mask

Correct. Both nostrils are packed, so a nasal cannula would not deliver. Her hypoxia is mild at 89%, and she is comfortable otherwise. A simple mask, a low flow device that covers the nose and mouth, can still deliver oxygen, at 5-10 L/min.
Nasal cannula at 2 L/min

A nasal cannula delivers through the nostrils, and both are packed, so oxygen cannot enter. The cannula is a common choice for mild hypoxia, but it relies on a patent nose. Tell: when the nose is blocked, use a device that covers the mouth.
ruled out by a stated finding

set2.io: Explain the rationale for a nebulizer treatment.
set2.q: A 52-year-old woman with chronic lung disease has thick secretions she struggles to cough up during a severe exacerbation. Besides medication delivery, which listed rationale for a nebulizer applies?
opts: Secretion clearance

Correct. Her thick secretions that she cannot cough up in a severe exacerbation match secretion clearance, which is a listed rationale for a nebulizer along with delivering liquid medication directly to the airways. The nebulizer helps move the mucus.
Delivering a fixed oxygen fraction

Delivering a fixed oxygen fraction is a feature of air-entrainment devices such as the Venturi mask, which hold the fraction steady regardless of demand. It is not the stated reason for a nebulizer, and it does not address her secretions. Tell: the fixed fraction is about oxygen; her problem is mucus.
confused mechanism or drug class
Preventing carbon dioxide retention

Preventing carbon dioxide retention is not a listed rationale for a nebulizer. Carbon dioxide retention is a hazard of oxygen therapy, and her stem describes a mucus problem. Tell: the nebulizer is for medication and secretion clearance, not for guarding against hypercapnia.
confused mechanism or drug class
Replacing her need for oxygen

A nebulizer delivers liquid medication to the airways and does not replace oxygen. If she needs oxygen she still requires an oxygen delivery device. Tell: a nebulizer carries medication and helps clear secretions; oxygen delivery is a separate need.
common lay belief

set2.io: Identify the indications, benefits, and hazards of oxygen therapy.
set2.q: A 38-year-old man has attacks of severe one-sided headache around his eye, each lasting under an hour, several days in a row. His saturation is 99%. Which therapy is a listed special indication for him?
opts: No oxygen, since he is not hypoxic

A saturation of 99% would justify withholding oxygen only for hypoxia. Cluster headache and air hunger are the two special indications that apply even when the patient is not hypoxic. Tell: for these two special indications, oxygen is given despite a normal saturation.
ruled out by a stated finding
A bag-valve mask

A bag-valve mask is a resuscitator for a patient who is not breathing adequately, and he is breathing normally. It has nothing to do with a headache. Tell: the resuscitator is for failed ventilation; cluster headache is relieved by oxygen.
ruled out by a stated finding
Oxygen therapy

Correct. Severe one-sided headaches around the eye, brief and recurring daily for days, fit cluster headache, which is a listed special indication for oxygen. His saturation of 99% does not matter, because the indication here is the headache, not hypoxia.
Nebulized saline

Nebulized saline is not a listed therapy for cluster headache. A nebulizer delivers liquid medication directly to the airways, for medication choice or secretion clearance. Tell: nebulizers treat airway problems; cluster headache is one of the two special indications for oxygen.
adjacent fact

set2.topic: Reading the fraction from the flow
set2.io: Compare and contrast the different oxygen delivery systems.
set2.q: A 75-year-old man's family turned his home nasal cannula up to 9 L/min because he felt short of breath. About what fraction of inspired oxygen does he receive at that setting?
opts: Correct. A nasal cannula can be turned to any setting, but the fraction stops at 44% (reached at 6 L/min). At 9 L/min he gets no more than that, so the extra 3 liters add oxygen to his nose but not to his fraction.

56% would follow from continuing to add 4% per liter, but the cannula's fraction maxes out at 44%. The knob can turn over 6 L/min, yet the fraction does not rise. Tell: the cannula has a ceiling; the arithmetic stops at 6 L/min.
reversed direction or value
60% belongs to the low end of a non-rebreather mask's 60-100% range at 10-15 L/min. A cannula does not reach it. Tell: you need a reservoir bag device to get above 44%.
reversed direction or value
100% is the top of the non-rebreather's range, requiring a reservoir bag and 10-15 L/min. A cannula at 9 L/min cannot reach it. Tell: the cannula is a low flow device with a hard ceiling of 44%.
reversed direction or value

set2.io: Discuss the selection and application of oxygen delivery
set2.q: A 65-year-old woman has a daytime saturation of 95%. Overnight oximetry shows her falling to 91% at the lowest. Does she qualify for nocturnal oxygen?
opts: Yes, since she drops during sleep

Dropping during sleep is not enough. The criterion needs a saturation of 88% or less and a drop of 5% or more. Hers falls only 4%, to 91%, which is still above 88%. Tell: both the level and the size of the drop must be met.
ruled out by a stated finding
Yes, in Group II

Group II is the resting category for a saturation of 89% (or arterial oxygen pressure of 56-59 mm Hg) plus pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale or a hematocrit above 56%. It does not turn a sleep value of 91% into a qualification. Tell: Group II is about resting values with a comorbidity.
adjacent fact
Yes, if she also has diabetes

Diabetes is not a qualifying comorbidity on the list, which names pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale and polycythemia. It would not change a sleep value that fails both thresholds. Tell: her numbers decide, and they fall short.
adjacent fact
No, her sleep value stays above 88%

Correct. Sleep qualification needs a saturation of 88% or less with a drop of 5% or more from baseline. Her lowest value of 91% is above 88%, and 95 minus 91 is only a 4% drop. She fails both parts, so she does not qualify.

set2.io: Identify the indications, benefits, and hazards of oxygen therapy.
set2.q: An 84-year-old woman in hospice with metastatic cancer has air hunger (a distressing sense of not getting enough breath). Her saturation is 95%. Which therapy is a listed special indication?
opts: An endotracheal tube

An endotracheal tube is an advanced airway placed in the trachea. Her complaint is the sensation of breathlessness, and an airway device is not the listed therapy for it. Tell: air hunger is relieved by oxygen for symptom relief.
wrong stage or severity
Oxygen for symptom relief

Correct. The hospice patient has air hunger, a distressing sense of not getting enough breath, and a saturation of 95%. Air hunger is a listed special indication, and symptom relief is a listed benefit of oxygen, so oxygen is given for comfort even without hypoxia.
No oxygen, since saturation is normal

Normal saturation does not exclude oxygen here. Air hunger and cluster headache are the special indications, and symptom relief is a listed benefit. Tell: for air hunger the goal is relief of the sensation, so a reading of 95% does not settle it.
ruled out by a stated finding
A home oxygen qualification test

A home oxygen qualification test documents hypoxia during rest, exertion or sleep using a saturation or arterial gas value. Her saturation is 95%, and the listed indication here is air hunger, not documented hypoxia. Tell: qualification documents hypoxia for home oxygen; air hunger is a special indication in itself.
wrong stage or severity

set2.io: Discuss the selection and application of oxygen delivery
set2.q: A 69-year-old woman with chronic lung disease drops from 94% to 86% while walking. Oxygen at 2 and then 4 L/min is added, but her saturation stays at 86% while walking. How does this result bear on ambulatory oxygen?
opts: It does not meet the exertion criterion

Correct. Her saturation falls from 94% to 86% on walking, which is at or below 88%. But the exertion criterion also requires that the saturation improves when oxygen is given, and at 2 and 4 L/min it stays at 86%, so she does not meet the exertion criterion.
It qualifies her for ambulatory oxygen

The drop to 86% satisfies only half the criterion. Exertion qualification needs the saturation to improve with oxygen, and hers did not improve at 2 or 4 L/min. Tell: a drop alone does not qualify; the improvement with oxygen is required.
ruled out by a stated finding
It qualifies her in Group I at rest

Group I is for a resting saturation of 88% or less on room air. Her resting value was 94%, and her problem is only on exertion, so she does not qualify at rest. Tell: Group I is about rest; her low value appears only with walking.
adjacent fact
It qualifies her for sleep oxygen

The sleep criterion is a saturation of 88% or less with a drop of 5% or more from baseline. Her stem describes walking, not sleep. Tell: the exertion test is the one that applies here, and it was not met.
adjacent fact

set2.io: Compare and contrast the different oxygen delivery systems.
set2.q: A 54-year-old man with severe pneumonia is on an aerosol mask from an air-entrainment nebulizer. The team wants to raise its fraction to 0.80. Why is that setting a concern?
opts: It cannot go above 0.28
This device is not capped at 0.28. It can deliver higher fractions, and the concern is the specific recommendation not to go above 0.50. Tell: the limit is a recommended ceiling of 0.50, not 0.28.
reversed direction or value
It is recommended above 0.50
The recommendation is the opposite: use above 0.50 is not recommended. Reading it as recommended would invert the ceiling. Tell: 0.50 is a ceiling, not a floor.
reversed direction or value
It changes with his breathing rate

An air-entrainment system gives a fixed fraction that does not fluctuate with patient demand. A fraction that follows breathing rate describes the cannula, simple mask or non-rebreather. Tell: air entrainment is steady; the concern with 0.80 is the recommended ceiling.
confused mechanism or drug class
It is not recommended above 0.50

Correct. A fixed-fraction air-entrainment nebulizer can deliver higher fractions, but setting above 0.50 is not recommended. His team wants 0.80, which is beyond that ceiling, so it is a concern even though his pneumonia is severe.

set2.io: Discuss patient education for oxygen delivery
set2.q: A 66-year-old man on home oxygen restores old cars in his garage and rubs grease off his hands with an oil-based cleanser while wearing his cannula. Which teaching applies?
opts: Use a Venturi mask when working

A Venturi mask is a high flow device that gives a precise fraction, often used in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. It would not remove the petroleum product hazard. Tell: the teaching concerns what touches the oxygen, not which mask he wears.
adjacent fact
Avoid petroleum-based oils and grease

Correct. Home oxygen teaching is to avoid petroleum-based products such as lip balms, lotions, oils and grease. He is wearing his cannula while rubbing grease off with an oil-based cleanser, so he should avoid those petroleum oils and grease.
Turn the flow up while working

Turning the flow up does not remove the petroleum product; the teaching is to avoid petroleum-based oils and grease, not to change the flow. Tell: the fix is to change the product, not the oxygen setting.
reversed direction or value
Wear a simple mask in the garage

A simple mask is a low flow device for mild to moderate respiratory distress. He has no respiratory problem described, and changing the mask would not address the grease. Tell: his hazard is the product on his hands.
adjacent fact

set2.io: Evaluate the patient’s response to oxygen therapy.
set2.q: A 60-year-old man with heart failure is on oxygen while his fluid overload is treated. Over two days his breathing eases, his saturation stays at target, and his vital signs settle. Which ongoing step is part of evaluating his oxygen therapy?
opts: Start home oxygen qualification today

Home oxygen qualification is performed at the time of need, with documentation of hypoxia at rest, exertion or sleep, when a patient is going home. He is still in treatment for fluid overload. Tell: qualification is about home coverage, not about evaluating his current response.
wrong stage or severity
Keep monitoring for complications

Correct. Evaluating response ends with vital signs and further monitoring for complications. His breathing has eased and his saturation holds, but he remains on oxygen, so the hazards of oxygen therapy still need watching.
Stop checking his saturation
Stopping saturation checks would drop the objective data used to judge response. The target varies, but the measurement continues. Tell: stable results are a reason to keep monitoring, not to stop.
wrong stage or severity
Raise his flow to secure the gains
Raising the flow when he is already at target would add oxygen he does not need and risk its hazards. His saturation stays at target. Tell: at target, the plan is to monitor, not to increase.
reversed direction or value
